content: The 90–90–90 treatment target is a global initiative aimed at addressing the HIV epidemic. It focuses on three key goals: ensuring that 90% of all people living with HIV (PLHIV) are diagnosed, 90% of those diagnosed are receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and 90% of those on ART achieve viral suppression. These targets are designed to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality and to ultimately end the AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. To monitor progress toward these targets, a comprehensive framework of global indicators has been established. These indicators assess the health service cascade, which includes diagnosis, treatment, and viral suppression, as well as the impact of these services on HIV incidence and mortality. The framework also emphasizes the importance of identifying bottlenecks in the cascade and implementing targeted actions to address them. The health service cascade can be analyzed using two primary methods: cohort-based and cross-sectional approaches. A cohort-based HIV cascade follows a specific group of individuals diagnosed with HIV over time, tracking their progression through diagnosis, care, ART initiation, and viral suppression. This method requires unique patient identifiers and electronic data management systems to link information across multiple service delivery points. It provides detailed insights into the effectiveness of linkages between services and patient retention in care. In contrast, a cross-sectional HIV cascade provides a snapshot of the continuum of care at a specific point in time. It aggregates data on the number of people living with HIV, those diagnosed, those receiving care, those on ART, and those who are virally suppressed. While this method does not track individual patients, it offers valuable insights into the overall program response and effectiveness at different stages of the cascade. The 90–90–90 targets are ambitious but achievable. By 2020, the goal was to diagnose 90% of all PLHIV, ensure 90% of those diagnosed are on ART, and achieve viral suppression in 90% of those on ART. Achieving these targets would result in 73% of all PLHIV being virally suppressed, a critical milestone in ending the AIDS epidemic. However, not all countries have monitoring systems capable of directly measuring these targets, particularly the number of PLHIV who have been diagnosed. As a result, ART coverage among all PLHIV is often used as a proxy for the second 90 target. To improve monitoring and accountability, the framework prioritizes indicators for global reporting and routine program management. It also emphasizes the need for disaggregated data by age, sex, key populations, and location to better understand the epidemic and tailor interventions. Regular impact evaluations are essential to ensure programs are focused on reducing HIV incidence and mortality and to make necessary adjustments to improve outcomes. The HIV care cascade highlights the importance of linking data across the continuum of care. For example, the number of people in HIV care can be counted, but it may not always be possible to link these individuals to their diagnosis records. Despite these challenges, creating cascades from aggregate data can still provide a useful snapshot of the current situation and inform program improvements. The momentum around the 90–90–90 targets has grown as the international community transitions from the Millennium Development Goals to the Sustainable Development Goals. UNAIDS has worked with partners to build global consensus on these targets, which are critical for bringing HIV treatment to all who need it. Modeling suggests that achieving these targets, along with prevention efforts, will end the AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. To support these efforts, strategic information guidelines have been developed to consolidate data and improve monitoring. These guidelines outline key indicators along the HIV cascade and provide practical considerations for their use. They also stress the importance of linking data to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the epidemic and the effectiveness of interventions. By focusing on these priorities, countries can strengthen their HIV response and accelerate progress toward ending the epidemic.
